Entries here concern `realm/blong-chat`; anything cross-cutting belongs in the repository-root
memory.

## Open

### F-638 — The dev intent puts the gateway on a random port

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · open_

A suite entry that configures gateway.port 8080 still listens on a random port under dev, because
the framework's dev block merges after the suite's default and sets port 0 so two processes on one
machine do not collide. A live check has to read the port from the log line or
pass --gateway.port=8080 on the command line; the realm's own index.ts comment now says so instead
of promising 8080.

### F-641 — A handler's config is its group slice, not the realm block

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · open_

A handler's closure config is the slice of the group folder it sits in (`chat.in`, `chat.out`), not
the realm's own config block, while `this.config` inside the handler is the config of the port the
method was dispatched on. The realm's setting therefore has to live under the port's name
(`chat.chatDispatch.forward`) or be read from the port, and a handler reading `config.forward` from
a realm-level block gets `undefined` with no warning — which is how a forward seam silently did
nothing while the inbound tests timed out. The path to the answer runs through layerProxy's
`createHandlerClosure(others, moduleConfig.name, moduleConfig[name], ...)`: `moduleConfig` is the
realm block, so `moduleConfig[groupFolder]` is what a closure sees. Read that line before debugging
why a config value is missing.

### F-643 — A realm-layer simulator reads its config from inside the realm block

> _2026-10-30 · realm/blong-chat · open_

A simulator port's own settings live inside the realm's block, not at the top level: `slackSim: {}`
gates the layer file's loading, but the port reads `server.port` from `chat.slackSim`, because a
realm-layer port's config slice is that realm's block indexed by the file's base name. Overriding
the top-level block silently did nothing and the run kept binding the simulator's default port,
which reads as "the override was ignored" until the slice is traced. Same rule as a realm's own
adapter (`chat.slack`), and the practical test is whether the value appears in the port's `config`
at `ready`.

### F-644 — The suite and a running dev process want the same fixed ports

> _2026-10-30 · realm/blong-chat · open_

A developer's `blong` process in the realm loads dev _and_ integration, so it binds the listeners,
the gateway and both simulators — exactly the ports a `blong-dev test` run wants, and the suite died
with EADDRINUSE while the other process was serving Slack through ngrok. The fix is
`CHAT_TEST_PORT`, one variable that moves the whole set (listeners, simulators and the test accounts
that call them) in one step; a single number moved alone only shifts the collision. The general
lesson for a realm with fixed listener ports: give the test run one knob that moves every address it
owns.

### F-663 — An adapter folder handler is not reachable by dispatch from another realm

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-chat · open_

Handlers under `adapter/db` are reached by injection from a handler in the same realm, but a
dispatch to the same method name from another realm resolved without running it and without an
error, so a binding write looked successful and wrote nothing. Serving the same method from a group
on the orchestrator, which calls the db handler by injection, is what made it reachable. Watch for a
leg name that never appears in the log: no leg, no handler.

### F-666 — The forward map is keyed by account alias, not by platform

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-chat · open_

A chat deployment that wrote `forward: {slack: agent.chat.receive}` sent every message to the `*`
entry, because the realm asks the map for the account that received the message. The symptom is a
real workspace where the bot is silent and the logs show the HTTP request and nothing else, and the
simulator test never caught it because it called the consumer directly instead of going through the
inbound handler. Key the map by the alias (`blong-bot`) or use `*`, and assert at least once through
`chat.in.message.receive` rather than past it.

### F-668 — A re-pointed Slack app can be left pointing at a dead tunnel

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-chat · open_

A run whose account carries a config token rewrites the app Request URL to whatever tunnel it
discovered, and ngrok hands out a new hostname per session. When the agent or the tunnel dies the
app keeps posting to the old host, so every real message is delivered to nothing and the realm looks
broken while it is simply never addressed. Check the configured URL with apps.manifest.export before
debugging the realm, and compare it with the tunnel that is running. The framework side of the same
lesson is that the webhook acknowledges first and detaches, so a delivery that goes nowhere leaves
no trace in the realm at all.

### F-669 — A dispatch to a namespace in the same process still left it

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-chat · open_

A webhook answers the platform before the realm runs, so the hop to its destination is detached;
without `remote.canSkipSocket` that hop leaves the process for a socket address only a cluster has,
hangs, and the message is lost with the 200 already sent. The symptom is a real Slack workspace
where the bot never replies and the console says nothing, while the same code passes every simulator
test because `integration` sets the flag. A deployment intent that serves every namespace in one
process has to set it too.

### F-717 — A realm restated the port default, hiding it live

> _2026-11-11 · realm/blong-chat · open_

The live check said the card was rendered inline, and the deployed realm was the reason:
`chatPromptAsk` filled `presentation: params.presentation ?? 'inline'`, so the port's own default
could never be reached from a realm caller — the tap suite passed because it calls the realm, not
the port. Two lessons. A default that belongs to the port must not be restated by a caller; spread
the field only when it is present
(`...(params.presentation && {presentation: params.presentation})`), and let the port decide. And a
live check is the only way to see a default being overridden: sim tests asserted the port and could
not see the realm's filler. The tests that encoded the old surface now name `presentation: 'inline'`
explicitly, since they are about the reply path and the plain controls rather than about the
default.

## Resolved

### F-642 — A nested handler's error arrives as a value, not a rejection

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · resolved_

A handler that throws `errors[name]({params}, $meta)` answers an array, and a caller one hop below
the request boundary receives that array as a resolved value rather than a rejection:
`chatPromptAsk` awaited `chatOutMessageSend` for a Viber multi-choice, the port refused it, and the
ask still waited for its timeout, so the test read `chatPromptTimeout` where the log plainly said
`viber.controlUnsupported`. The fix is to inspect what came back (`sendFailure` in
`chatPromptAsk.ts`) instead of trusting the rejection, and the lesson is that a nested `handler()`
call's failure may be a value — check it at the place where the failure has to become the caller's
answer. The second shape turned up when the echo was added: a failure the _port_ meets on the reply
(Slack answering `ok: false`) comes back as the error object itself, with no array around it, so
`sendFailure` reads `Array.isArray(sent) ? sent[0] : sent` — a check that only unwrapped arrays
silently read a refused message as a success, and a refused question as one that had been delivered.

Both shapes are handled in `sendFailure`, and a refused question now fails the ask at once.

### F-646 — A platform limit was assumed, not read, and it shaped the default

> _2026-10-30 · realm/blong-chat · resolved_

The first pass decided that "Slack cannot render checkboxes or a text input in a message" and sent
every multiple choice and every free-text question behind a Choose button that opened a modal; the
comment in `blocks.ts` said so as if it were Slack's rule, and nobody checked it against the
reference. The premise is half wrong: checkboxes and radio buttons are listed as compatible elements
of an `actions` block and are available in messages, and only the text input needs the modal path.
The cost was a default a person has to click through twice for every question, and it took the user
trying the feature live to say so. The lesson is to read the surface list on the element's own
reference page before designing around a limitation — `available_in_surfaces` and
`compatible_elements` are printed on every Block Kit page — and to keep a claim about a platform in
an entry that can be retested rather than in a comment that reads as fact.

The default is inline now, and the platform rule is asserted in the port tests rather than assumed.

### F-650 — A wrong example looked like a missing protocol feature

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-chat · resolved_

The chat realm's own `.http` examples sent `params: [{...}]`, copied from the internal RPC server's
shape, and the first call failed validation. The repair I reached for was to make the _gateway_
accept both forms, as a JSON-RPC conformance argument — and it went into `Gateway.ts` as a
body-schema union plus an unwrap, with a test. It was asked for, so it was not wrong to consider; it
was wrong to do without checking who else sent the array form, because the answer was nobody: the
one committed example that looked like it (`demo/blong-hello`) has no exported `Handler` type, so no
schema validated it, the array was handed to a handler that ignored its argument, and the example
had been passing by accident. The cost was paid by every realm — each gateway route's published body
schema became `anyOf` — for a caller shape the framework never promised. The lesson is to price a
protocol change by who it serves and what it shows: an example that disagrees with the contract is
the thing to fix, and the cheaper question ("what does the other API do with params?") is exactly
the one that produces a wrong answer, because two surfaces can share a word and not a meaning.

Reverted: the gateway keeps by-name params (`@@D-698`), and the examples that disagreed were fixed
instead.

### F-712 — conversations.create answers fatal_error for a missing channel scope

> _2026-11-11 · realm/blong-chat · resolved_

Opening a Slack channel from a plan failed with `ok: false, error: fatal_error` from
`conversations.create`, which reads as a malformed request. The bot token was valid — `auth.test`
answered the team and the bot id — and both a private and a public create failed the same way.

The cause was a missing bot scope, `channels:manage` and `groups:write`, which Slack normally
reports as `missing_scope` with the needed and provided lists. It did not here, so the diagnosis
cost the manifest inspection that showed the app had been created with four chat scopes and no
channel one.

The lesson is that a Slack capability has to be proven against the live workspace before a task that
depends on it is called done: the simulator answers every method, so a tap suite cannot see a scope
gap. Add the scope, reinstall the app, and only then trust the call.

The app now carries both scopes; the manifest draft asks for them, so a new app is created with
them, and README says an installed app must be reinstalled.
